subject: Software Development

assessmentTargets.concept: Identify the command to verify Git is installed and interpret its output
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: So the first command you have is Git version. So if you want to know if the Git is installed in your system, then we will be using this particular command called as Git version.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to type the command and explain what the displayed version number indicates.

assessmentTargets.concept: Explain why global user name and email are required and how to set them with git config
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Git config is a command which is used to give details, give your details to the Git tool... you have to give your details like your username, your email ID... you have to give git config space hyphen hyphen global.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Segment describing git config Global Configuration
assessmentTargets.instruction: Prompt the learner to write the exact git config commands for name and email.

assessmentTargets.concept: Create a new local repository using the appropriate command and describe the result
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one you are using is Git init. ... you have to use a command called as git init. ... it will tell you that an empty repository has been created.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Segment describing git init Repository Initialization
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to run git init in a new folder and report the console message.

assessmentTargets.concept: Use git status to list staged, unstaged, and untracked changes in a repository
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next command you have is git status. ... it will tell you what are the changes that you have made and which changes have not yet been saved into the repository.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Segment describing git status Working Tree Inspection
assessmentTargets.instruction: Provide a scenario with modified files and ask the learner to interpret the git status output.

assessmentTargets.concept: Compare the current working tree with the previous commit using git diff and explain the output
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one is git diff. So for example, if you want to know what is the previous commit changes that I have made and what is the new chang
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to run git diff after making a change and describe what the diff shows.

reserveTargets.concept: Stage specific files using git add and explain its effect on the index
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: The next one you have is git add. So this is, if you remember in your git workflow, I told you we have three areas. Working directory, stagi
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: Observed teaching behavior explaining git add
reserveTargets.instruction: Have the learner add a file and verify its staged status with git status.

reserveTargets.concept: Create a new commit with git commit and describe what metadata is recorded
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: Then you have to go for the next one, which is called as git commit. Git commit will save the changes of your particular file into the repos
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: Observed teaching behavior reinforcing git commit
reserveTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to commit staged changes and view the commit log.

reserveTargets.concept: Execute the full workflow: add, commit, and then view differences with git diff
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: Combined evidence from git add, git commit, and git diff behaviors
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: Sequence of observed teaching behaviors covering add, commit, diff
reserveTargets.instruction: Present a mini project scenario and require the learner to complete the full workflow, explaining each step.
